newsitem.title: CHINA: HK Democrats blast handover government's polls plan.
newsitem.headline: HK Democrats blast handover government's polls plan.

text.p: Hong Kong's popular Democratic Party, winners of the biggest vote in the 1995 elections, slammed the new government on Friday over a balloting blueprint that would slash the party's electoral prospects.

Ousted Democratic Party legislator Lee Wing-tat attacked the government's draft election rules after meeting Constitutional Affairs Secretary Nicholas Ng to discuss next May's Legislative Council elections, the first under Chinese rule.
China resumed sovereignty over Hong Kong on July 1 after 156 years of British colonial rule.

"The (electoral) system wants to minimise the participation of the people and it also has a hidden political agenda, which is to reduce the number of seats that can be won by the Democratic Party," Lee said after meeting Ng.
Lee was one of 26 pro-democracy lawmakers tossed out of office when China took over Hong Kong and disbanded the elected legislature, replacing it with an appointed interim body.
The Democrat also criticised the shortness of a planned public consultation on the polling rules.
Many in Hong Kong have expressed fears of repressive communist-style rule in the territory of 6.4 million people, which is supposed to be a highly autonomous, special capitalist region of China.
Some recent developments, such as the post-colonial government's dilution of civil liberties and democracy, and a rollback of labour rights laws, have increased these concerns.
On Wednesday, the China-backed Hong Kong government announced a pulse-taking exercise to tap public views on the election law.
But the exercise would last only until next Thursday, and critics said this showed the government was insincere. Public consultations usually last for weeks, sometimes even months.
Lee said the public should have more time to study the implications of the proposed changes, which would see 39 of the 60 seats elected in an entirely new way.
A government official shrugged off the attack and said discussions on the arrangements had been going on for some time and "there have been ample opportunities for the public to air their views".

The official said the proposed changes were recommendations of the China-appointed Preparatory Committee, which was in charge of setting up the territory's transitional power structures. The committee has now been dissolved.
The new electoral blueprint proposes to give votes to corporations rather than individuals to elect legislators from 30 "functional constituencies".
More than two million people who were eligible to vote in the 1995 Legislative Council polls would be disenfranchised under the proposal. They would be replaced by corporate votes cast by companies.
